blocks.text: The use of honey in drink seems to be commended by these words of Nehemiah in Jerome's version [col. 526], ch. VIII, 10: Go, eat the fat, and drink mead. So it reads in Jerome. Mulsum [mead], however, is οἰνόμελι [oinomeli], that is, a drink made from wine and honey. The method of preparing it is accurately taught by Dioscorides, book 5, ch. 8, Palladius, book 11, ch. 17, and the authors of the Geoponica, book 8, ch. 25; Pliny also mentions it in passing, book 22, ch. 24. Nor did it escape the Talmudists in the tractate On Idolatry, ch. 2, fol. 30a, where, to the question what אינומלין, οἰνόμελι [oinomeli], is, they answer that it is יין ודבש ופלפלין, wine, and honey, and pepper, mixed and blended together. This description, however, rather belongs to conditum [spiced wine]. Finally, Macrobius, Saturnalia book 7, ch. 12, asks why mead is best blended from fresh honey and old wine. Mead is also frequently mentioned in the poets. Plautus in the Persa, Scene 3:
Mix the mead, get ready quinces and pears.
And in the Stichus, Act 2, Scene 1:
How many draughts of mead, and how many luncheons?
Horace, book 2, Satire 2:
Spurn cheap food, unless you drink Hymettian honey diluted with Falernian. — — —
And Satire 4:
Aufidius used to mix honey with strong Falernian, wrongly; for to empty veins one should commit nothing but what is mild: you will do better to wash your insides with mild mead. — — —
Virgil, book 4 of the Georgics, [III, 390] You will press sweet honey, not so much sweet as clear, and fit to tame the harsh taste of Bacchus.
That is, suited for mead (says Servius), because our ancestors tempered very harsh wines with the sweetness of honey. Martial, book 4, Epigram 13:
As well as rare cinnamon mixes with its ^{u)} nard, so well do Massic wines mix with Thesean honeycombs.
And book 13, Epigram 108:
You muddy nectar-like Falernian with Attic honey; such a drink deserves to be mixed by Ganymede.
Corippus, book 3:
They poured dark Risattic wines into the tawny metal, wines which nature prepares with no need of liquid honey.
They hold that Homer led the way, Iliad κ' [kappa], line 234, where Circe
— — — μέλι χλωρὸν Οἴνῳ Πραμνείῳ ἐκύκα, — — [meli chlōron / Oinō Pramneiō ekyka]

mixed fresh honey with Pramnian wine. Indeed, long before Circe, Aristaeus (they say) was the first of all to mix honey with wine. So Pliny, book 14, ch. 4. Yet Plutarch counts οἰνόμελι [oinomeli], mead, among things recently invented. The passage is Table Talk, book 8, Question 9: Πολλὰ γὰρ τῶν ἀγεύστων καὶ ἀβρώτων πρότερον, ἥδιστα νῦν γέγονεν, ὥσπερ οἰνόμελι, καὶ μήτρα· [Polla gar tōn ageustōn kai abrōtōn proteron, hēdista nyn gegonen, hōsper oinomeli, kai mētra] For many things which were formerly not tasted or eaten are now held to be most delicious, such as mead and sow's womb. Or is it because the gluttony of later times added so much to the inventions of the ancients that the thing could be considered new? Thus not even the name οἰνόμελι [oinomeli] occurs anywhere, so far as I know, before Dioscorides. And in the passage of Nehemiah cited above, the Hebrew has only שתו ממתקים, Drink sweet things, and the Greek version Πίετε γλυκάσματα [Piete glykasmata]. So also 3 Esdr. IX, 52.

The medicinal use of honey has already ^{x)} been treated, on those words of the Greek version about the bee, Proverb. VI, 8. Ἧς τοὺς πόνους βασιλεῖς τε καὶ ἰδιῶται πρὸς ὑγίειαν προσφέρονται [Hēs tous ponous basileis te kai idiōtai pros hygieian prospherontai], Whose labours (that is, honey) kings and private persons use for health. Add to these the passage on Jonathan, 1 Sam. XIV, 27: Stretching out the tip of the rod which he had in his hand, he dipped it in a honeycomb; and when he had put his hand to his mouth, his eyes regained their light. The Arabic adds لان كان اظلم [III, 391] عليه [li-an kāna aẓlama ʿalayhi] Because darkness had come over him. That is, through hunger, as with Plautus' Curculio, [col. 527] who, pressed by hunger, bursts out in these words, Act 2, Scene 3:
— darkness comes over me, my knees give way from hunger.
And a little later,
— — — I am done for, I can hardly see, my mouth is bitter, my teeth clogged, my throat bleary with hunger.

To have one's sight darkened by hunger is said in Arabic اسدف [asdafa] asdapha, a most proper verb. Further, as the distinguished Vossius rightly observes on this passage, book 4 On Idolatry, ch. 79, while all food has the property of restoring lost strength, honey, like wine, does this especially, because both are subtle and therefore diffuse their power more quickly. Some observe that it is a property of honey to dispel dimness of the eyes. Many ancients assert this: Dioscorides, book 2, on honey: Ἀποκαθαίρει δὲ τὰ ἐπισκοτοῦντα ταῖς κόραις· [Apokathairei de ta episkotounta tais korais] It cleanses away what brings dimness on the eyes. Pliny, book 29, ch. 6: Honey in which bees have died is most useful for the eyes. Serenus Sammonicus, ch. 14:
The juices of Hyblaean honey with goat's gall help eyes oppressed by dreadful darkness.
